title: Rocks and soil
keyIdea: Soil is not just crushed rock. It is a mix of tiny bits of rock, humus (dark, rotted plant and animal remains), water, air and living things such as worms and microbes. In a typical garden loam, about 45% is rock bits, 25% water, 25% air and 5% humus. The rock bits come in sizes: sand grains are the biggest, silt is smaller and clay bits are too tiny to see. Shake soil in a jar of water and the biggest bits sink first: sand at the bottom, then silt, then clay, with humus floating. Sandy soil has big gaps, so water drains through fast and it dries out. Clay soil has tiny gaps, so it holds water and can get waterlogged. Loam is a mix that suits most plants. Soil forms very slowly: rain, ice and roots break rock, and plants rot into humus. It can take up to 1,000 years to make 1 cm of soil.
familyTip: Do a shake test together. Half-fill a clear jar with garden soil, top it up with water, add the lid and shake hard. Leave it on a windowsill and look after a minute, an hour and a day. Ask which layer settled first and why, and what is floating on top.

visual.caption: Sandy soil or clay soil? Drag each fact into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Tiny bits, too small to see

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill a jar with the parts of soil, shake it and name the layers, pour water through three soils, match soils to jobs and order how soil is made.

kid: Dig up a spoon of soil and look closely. You will see tiny bits of rock, dark crumbly bits and maybe a worm. Soil is a mix. It has bits of rock, humus, water, air and living things. Humus is what is left when dead leaves, plants and animals rot.

The rock bits come in sizes. Sand grains are the biggest. You can feel them. Silt is smaller. Clay bits are so tiny you cannot see one on its own. Shake soil in a jar of water. The big sand grains sink first. Clay settles last, on top. Humus floats.

Sandy soil has big gaps between its grains, so water rushes through. It dries out fast. Clay soil has tiny gaps, so it holds water. It feels sticky when wet and cracks when dry. Loam is a mix of sand, silt, clay and humus. Most plants grow well in it.

Soil is made very slowly. Rain, ice and plant roots crack rock into bits. Plants grow, die and rot into humus. Worms mix it all together. It can take up to 1,000 years to make just 1 cm of soil. That is why we look after it.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. This is National Curriculum Year 3 Rocks: 'recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter', with the non-statutory suggestion to explore different kinds of soil. Key words: soil, humus, organic matter, sand, silt, clay, loam, drain, settle, weathering.

Facts used: USDA texture classes put sand at 0.05 to 2 mm, silt at 0.002 to 0.05 mm and clay under 0.002 mm. A typical loam is about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air by volume. The FAO (2015) says it can take up to 1,000 years to form 1 cm of soil, so soil is not quickly renewable. The 80, 50 and 15 ml in the lab's water test are a demonstration, in the order real drainage tests give.

Common mistakes: thinking soil is just crushed rock, or just 'dirt'; thinking the tiniest bits sink first in the shake test; thinking clay drains fastest because it feels smooth; thinking sand is best for all plants; and thinking soil forms in a few years. Some children also think worms eat rock. They do not, but they mix humus into the soil.

The lab has children fill a jar with soil's five parts (plastic and sugar are refused), shake it and name the layers bottom first, pour 100 ml through three soils and read the cylinders, match soils to jobs, and put the steps of soil-making in order.

practice.prompt: Rocks and soil: what is soil made of?
choices: Rock bits, humus, water, air and living things
practice.hint: Think of everything you can find in a spoon of garden soil.
practice.explain: Soil is a mix. It has rock bits and humus, with water and air in the gaps, and living things like worms and microbes.

practice.prompt: You pour {a}0 ml of water on sandy soil. {b}0 ml drains through. How many ml stayed in the soil?
practice.hint: Take the water that came out away from the water you poured in.
practice.explain: {a}0 − {b}0 = {=a*10-b*10} ml stayed in the soil. Sandy soil lets most water through.

practice.prompt: A garden bed has {n} cm of soil. It took about 500 years to make each cm. About how many years did it take?
practice.hint: Add 500 years once for each cm of soil.
practice.explain: {n} × 500 = {=n*500} years. Soil forms very slowly, so we look after it.

practice.prompt: You shake soil in a jar of water. What settles at the bottom first?
practice.hint: Which bits are biggest and heaviest?
practice.explain: Big, heavy sand grains sink first. Silt settles next and tiny clay bits settle last. Humus floats.

practice.prompt: Which soil lets water drain through fastest?
practice.hint: Which soil has the biggest gaps between its bits?
practice.explain: Sand grains are big, so the gaps between them are big. Water rushes through sandy soil.

pool.hint: It is the dark, crumbly part of soil.
pool.explain: Humus forms when dead leaves, plants and animals rot. It holds water and feeds plants.

pool.prompt: Why can clay soil get waterlogged?
choices: Its tiny bits leave tiny gaps for water
It has no rock in it
pool.hint: Think about the size of the gaps between clay bits.
pool.explain: Clay bits are tiny and packed close, so water moves through very slowly and the soil stays wet.

pool.prompt: Which soil is best for most vegetables?
pool.hint: Which soil is a mix that drains but still holds some water?
pool.explain: Loam mixes sand, silt, clay and humus. It drains well but holds enough water and food for most plants.

pool.prompt: How long can it take to make 1 cm of soil?
pool.hint: Rock breaks down very, very slowly.
pool.explain: The FAO says it can take up to 1,000 years to form 1 cm of soil, so soil lost to erosion is not quickly replaced.

pool.prompt: What starts to break rock into the bits that make soil?
pool.hint: Think of water freezing in a crack.
pool.explain: Rain wears rock away, water freezes and widens cracks, and roots push in. This breaking up is called weathering.

pool.prompt: 100 ml of water is poured on clay soil. Only {b} ml drains through. How many ml did the clay hold?
pool.hint: Take the water that drained away from 100 ml.
pool.explain: 100 − {b} = {=100-b} ml stayed in the clay. Clay holds water because its gaps are tiny.

pool.prompt: A jar of soil settles into layers: {s} cm of sand, {t} cm of silt and 1 cm of clay. How tall is the soil in the jar?
pool.explain: {s} + {t} + 1 = {=s+t+1} cm. Sand is at the bottom because its grains are the biggest.

pool.prompt: Ella says, 'Soil is just crushed-up rock.' What is missing?
choices: Humus, water, air and living things
pool.hint: What else did you put in the jar besides rock bits?
pool.explain: Rock bits are only about half of soil. It also has humus, water, air and living things like worms and microbes.

pool.prompt: Why is clay used to make pots?
choices: Wet clay is sticky and can be shaped
pool.hint: Think about how clay feels when it is wet.
pool.explain: Wet clay is sticky and holds its shape, and it goes hard when it is baked, so it makes good pots and bricks.
